You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Requirements:
        *   $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
    *   Best so far: `sshi_fbr` (score 79.31).
        *   Passed 5/6 conditions.
        *   Failed only S3 ripple: $V_{pp} = 61.1\text{mV}$ (limit $50\text{mV}$).
        *   S3 is the "strong excitation, light load" case ($I_p = 40\mu\text{A}$, $R_L = 22\text{k}\Omega$).

    *   Topology: SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) + Full Bridge Rectifier (FBR).
    *   Components:
        *   $L_1$ and $S_1$ (SYNC $G_1$) for inversion (flipping $C_p$ voltage).
        *   FBR ($D_1-D_4$) to rectify the voltage.
        *   $C_{out}$ for storage.
        *   $D_z$ (Zener) for clamping.
    *   Performance:
        *   The voltage settles around $3.3\text{V}$ for most cases.
        *   S3 ripple is just slightly too high ($61\text{mV}$ vs $50\text{mV}$).
        *   $C_{out}$ value was $209\text{nF}$.

    *   The only failure is ripple on S3.
    *   Ripple is $\Delta V \approx \frac{I \cdot \Delta t}{C_{out}}$.
    *   To decrease ripple, we can:
        1.  Increase $C_{out}$.
        2.  Decrease the charge pulse amplitude.
    *   However, increasing $C_{out}$ might increase $t_{up}$ (startup time).
    *   Wait, look at $t_{up}$ for `sshi_fbr`:
        *   S1: $0.0722\text{s}$
        *   S2: $0.0725\text{s}$
        *   S3: $0.0182\text{s}$
        *   S4: $0.119\text{s}$
        *   S5: $0.0865\text{s}$
        *   S6: $0.103\text{s}$
        *   All are well below the $0.4\text{s}$ limit.
    *   This means we have a lot of room to increase $C_{out}$ to reduce ripple without violating the startup time.

    *   The current `sshi_fbr` uses $C_{out} = 209\text{nF}$.
    *   S3 ripple is $61\text{mV}$. To get it below $50\text{mV}$, we might need $C_{out} \approx 300\text{nF} - 1\mu\text{F}$.
    *   But the current `sshi_fbr` was already "tuned" (48 evaluations). If the tuner didn't find a better $C_{out}$, maybe there's a limit?
    *   Looking at the tuning: $C_{out}$ was $209\text{nF}$. If the tuner tried $1\mu\text{F}$, it might have increased $t_{up}$ too much? No, $t_{up}$ is very low.
    *   Maybe the tuner balanced $C_{out}$ and other parameters?
    *   Wait, if the only problem is ripple on S3, and $t_{up}$ is very safe, simply increasing $C_{out}$ should work.
    *   *Self-Correction*: The tuner is an "evolution strategy" and should have found the best $C_{out}$. If it stopped at $209\text{nF}$, it's possible that increasing $C_{out}$ further started affecting $dv$ (settling) or other parameters.
    *   Let's check $dv$: $dv$ wasn't reported as failing for `sshi_fbr`.
    *   Wait, let's look at the ripple on S1, S2, S4, S5, S6: they are all $\sim 40\text{mV}$. S3 is $61\text{mV}$. S3 has the highest $I_p$ ($40\mu\text{A}$), which explains the higher ripple.

    *   Since the goal is a structural change ("new_topology" or "modify_topology"), and the only issue is S3 ripple, I can't just "change the value" in the prompt (the tuner does that). I need to propose a topology that handles the ripple better or provides a more stable output.
    *   Is there a way to modify the `sshi_fbr` structure to reduce ripple?
    *   Adding a small RC filter after the rectifier (essentially the `sshi_fbr_filter` attempt) failed miserably because the L-C filter was likely too slow or inefficient.
    *   What if I add a second capacitor in parallel? (That's just increasing $C_{out}$).
    *   What if I use a different rectifier?
    *   Current FBR uses 4 Schottky diodes. The voltage drop is $\sim 0.25\text{V}$.
    *   Wait, a standard SSHI usually works by flipping the capacitor. The FBR then rectifies.
    *   What if we add a small inductor in series with the output of the bridge (before $C_{out}$) to create a buck-like filter? (That's what `sshi_fbr_filter` tried, but it had an L-C filter and failed).
    *   Let's look at `sshi_fbr` again. The Zener $D_z$ clamps to $3.3\text{V}$.
    *   If the ripple is $61\text{mV}$ and the mean is $3.37\text{V}$, the peak is $3.37 + 0.03 = 3.4\text{V}$. This is well within the $3.6\text{V}$ limit.

    *   Since `sshi_fbr` is almost perfect, maybe a slightly different SSHI variation?
    *   Maybe an SSHI with a different rectifier? Or a different way to handle the storage?
    *   Actually, looking at the results of `sshi_fbr`, the only thing that failed was S3 ripple. If the tuner already optimized $C_{out}$ and it's still $61\text{mV}$, maybe the pulses are too large.
    *   What if I use a synchronous rectifier instead of diodes? (S-rectification).
    *   But I only have 2 SYNC controllers. One is already used for the SSHI flip. I could use the second one for rectification, but SSHI requires flipping at both extrema, and rectification requires switching at those same points.
    *   Wait, if I use a SYNC to flip (both edges), I can use another SYNC to steer the current.
    *   However, a simpler approach to reduce ripple is to increase the storage capacity. Since the tuner already did its best with $C_{out}$, maybe we can add a second storage stage or a different filter.
    *   Actually, the `sshi_fbr` topology is:
        $L_1$ from $pzp$ to $n_1$, $S_1$ from $n_1$ to $pzn$.
        FBR ($D_1-D_4$) from $pzp, pzn$ to $out$.
        $C_{out}$ from $out$ to $0$.
    *   This is a classic SSHI. The ripple is caused by the discrete charge packets being dumped into $C_{out}$ every half period.
    *   To reduce ripple:
        1.  More capacitance (Tuner tried).
        2.  Smaller packets (Lower $L$ or $t_{on}$? But that reduces power).
        3.  Smoothing (L-C filter).
    *   Wait, the `sshi_fbr_filter` had $L_2$ and $C_1$. Maybe it was just too complex or poorly placed.
    *   Let's try a simpler filter: just a small inductor $L_{out}$ between the FBR and $C_{out}$.
        `pzp` $\to$ FBR $\to$ `n_rect` $\to$ $L_{out}$ $\to$ `out` $\to$ $C_{out} \to 0$.
        This creates a second-order filter.

    *   Let's consider an alternative: A charge pump or a different SSHI variant.
    *   But `sshi_fbr` is so close. Let's try to refine the filtering.
    *   What if we add a RC filter? $R_{filter}$ between the bridge and $C_{out}$.
        $pzp \to$ FBR $\to$ $n_{rect} \to R_{filter} \to$ `out` $\to$ $C_{out} \to 0$.
        This would reduce the peak current into $C_{out}$ and smooth the ripple.
        However, the $R_{filter}$ would cause a voltage drop. With $R_L \approx 10\text{k}\Omega$, the load current is $\approx 1.8\text{V} / 10\text{k}\Omega = 180\mu\text{A}$. A $100\Omega$ resistor would drop $18\text{mV}$. This is acceptable.
        But the charge pulses from the SSHI are much larger than the load current.
        $Q_{pulse} = C_p \cdot \Delta V$. For $C_p=25\text{nF}$ and $\Delta V=2\text{V}$, $Q=50\text{nC}$.
        The pulse duration is short. An RC filter might work.

    *   Let's try "sshi_fbr_rc_filter":
        - $L_1, S_1, G_1$ (SSHI flip)
        - FBR ($D_1-D_4$) $\to$ node `mid`
        - $R_1$ from `mid` to `out`
        - $C_{out}$ from `out` to $0$
        - $D_z$ from `out` to $0$

    *   Wait, another thought: $V_{pp}$ for S3 was $61\text{mV}$. If I just increase $C_{out}$ by 20%, it should drop to $50\text{mV}$. Why didn't the tuner do that?
    *   Maybe the tuner was limited by $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$?
    *   For S3, $V_{avg} = 3.37\text{V}$, $V_{max} = 3.39\text{V}$. The ripple is $61\text{mV}$, so $V_{peak} = 3.37 + 0.03 = 3.4\text{V}$.
    *   Wait, $V_{max}$ is the absolute maximum. $3.4\text{V}$ is fine.
    *   Maybe the tuner was limited by $t_{up}$? S3 $t_{up}$ is $0.018\text{s}$. Plenty of room.
    *   Maybe the tuner was limited by $dv$ (settling)?
    *   $dv$ is the difference between the mean of $0.6-0.7\text{s}$ and $0.7-0.8\text{s}$.
    *   If $C_{out}$ is too large, the capacitor takes longer to charge, and $dv$ might be $> 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   Let's check: For $C_{out} = 209\text{nF}$, the time constant $\tau = R_L \cdot C_{out} \approx 10\text{k}\Omega \cdot 200\text{nF} = 2\text{ms}$.
    *   $2\text{ms}$ is very fast. $dv$ should not be an issue even with $C_{out} = 10\mu\text{F}$.
    *   Wait, the `sshi_fbr` results say "conditions passed 5/6". The only fail is S3 ripple. This means $dv$ passed for all!
    *   This is very strange. If $dv$ passed and $t_{up}$ passed and $V_{max}$ passed, why didn't the tuner just increase $C_{out}$ more to fix the ripple?
    *   Maybe the tuner hit a local optimum? Or maybe the $C_{out}$ range was limited? (The range is $1\text{e-10}$ to $4.7\text{e-05}$ F).
    *   $C_{out} = 209\text{nF}$ is well within $47\mu\text{F}$.

    *   Is there another topology that is more robust?
    *   Let's try a "Differential SSHI" or a "Synchronous SSHI".
    *   Actually, let's try adding a small inductor $L_{out}$ in a way that it's more like a buck converter.
